source.title: Distinguishing the neural correlates of episodic memory encoding and semantic memory retrieval.

confidence_rationale: Shows episodic and semantic memory processes are dissociable yet INTERACT within shared prefrontal/temporal regions -- the mid-LIPFC serves both, and anterior episodic regions only engage when semantic retrieval is also high. Supports the 'shared substrate with partially-distinct components' reading (ARC-085) over fully parallel machineries. Discounted because it concerns the episodic-encoding/semantic-retrieval interaction rather than the autobiographical/semantic distinction directly.
failure_signatures: Anterior left inferior PFC was involved in episodic encoding only when semantic retrieval was also high -- the two memory operations are not separable in practice, undercutting a model in which an autobiographical type and a semantic type operate as independent stores.

mapping.source_claim_statement: Episodic encoding and semantic retrieval have dissociable neural correlates but interact in specific left temporal and prefrontal regions, with shared mid-ventrolateral PFC involvement and interdependence between the two operations.
mapping.ree_translation: Supports treating semantic and autobiographical/episodic content as components of ONE memory substrate with shared machinery (ARC-085's single-substrate thesis) rather than independent first-class types, reinforcing the parsimony argument behind the Q-060 tag-not-type decision.
mapping.mapping_caveat: This paper tests episodic-encoding vs semantic-retrieval, not autobiographical-vs-semantic content per se; the interaction it documents is suggestive of substrate-sharing but is one step removed from the specific autobiographical taxonomy question Q-060 asks.
mapping.source_context: Human factorial fMRI, n=18 adults, separating encoding-success from retrieval-success effects.

confidence_components.notes: Well-cited Cabeza-lab design; the low mapping fidelity reflects that the autobiographical dimension is inferred, not measured.
